diagnosis_steps: Map the alert IP to NFS shard number and cloud instance ID
Check instance reachability status in cloud console (often 'Instance reachability check failed')
Test the NFS port directly: nc -w 10 -v <ip> 2049
If SSH works: systemctl status nfs-server && systemctl status edge-agent
Check nfsd kernel threads: grep ^th /proc/net/rpc/nfsd (default 80 is often too low)
Check for processes stuck in uninterruptible sleep: ps -eo state,pid,cmd | grep '^D' (many D-state nfsd processes = hung NFS, load average will be very high)
resolution_steps: If instance reachability failed OR many D-state processes: reboot the instance (service restart will NOT recover a hung NFS - learned from experience)
After boot: verify nfs-server and edge-agent services are active
Post command outputs in thread, mark alert resolved
gotchas: Restarting nfs-server.service does not fix hung nfsd processes in D state; only a reboot clears them
Alert may re-fire within an hour if root cause is network-level; monitor load after reboot
If /etc/exports fails to read or /opt/<datadir>/nfs is missing, the data volume may not have mounted at boot - check lsblk and remount before starting nfs-server
example_commands: systemctl status nfs-server && systemctl status edge-agent

diagnosis_steps: Identify PVC name and namespace from alert labels
Check current usage percent and capacity: kubectl get pvc -n <ns>
Check fill trend on the storage dashboard - is it steady growth or a spike from a running job?
Verify the StorageClass allows expansion: kubectl get sc <class> -o jsonpath='{.allowVolumeExpansion}'
Check resize history - a PVC resized repeatedly indicates a leak, escalate to app owner instead
resolution_steps: Patch PVC to add ~20-25% capacity: kubectl patch pvc <name> -n <ns> -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"<new>Gi"}}}}'
Watch for FileSystemResizePending condition; some volume types need a pod restart to grow the filesystem
Verify free space recovered (target: back above 25-30% free)
Post before/after dashboard screenshots in thread
gotchas: PVCs can only grow, never shrink
Scratch-storage PVCs for transcode workloads fill during large jobs and may self-recover; check whether the writing job is about to finish before resizing

diagnosis_steps: Identify the target group from alert labels (commonly the haproxy/api target groups)
Check whether the unhealthy target is a newly launched instance still warming up
Check target health reason codes in the load balancer console/API
resolution_steps: If newly launched instance: wait and re-check within 10 minutes - usually passes health checks after warm-up
If still unhealthy: check instance system logs and the service on the failing port
Post before/after target-health screenshots in thread
gotchas: Most occurrences self-resolve as new autoscaled instances finish warming up; avoid acting in the first 5-10 minutes

diagnosis_steps: Query logs for upstream 5xx: filter upstreamStatus >= 500 AND <= 599 over the alert window
Group by proxyUpstreamName to find which service is failing (graphql-server, edge-controller, etc.)
Check whether pods for that service restarted or were rescheduled at the same time
Count total 5xx - a handful during a deploy/restart differs from a sustained failure
resolution_steps: If correlated with pod restarts: monitor until success rate recovers, document the restart cause
If sustained: check upstream pod logs and resource saturation; consider scaling the affected service
Post log samples and the log-search link in thread
gotchas: Status 531 with huge requestSize values usually indicates oversized client payloads, not a platform fault
Success-rate alerts in low-traffic regions can fire on a tiny absolute number of errors - always check the absolute 5xx count
